subject: Substituting a Reference Genetic Map for a given Actual Genetic Map

messages.author: c21014a119b81c26
messages.subject: Substituting a Reference Genetic Map for a given Actual Genetic Map
parts:
R/qtl Group:

I have a couple of questions for the R/qtl group, but first some background.  

A Soybean Reference Genetic Map was constructed with JoinMap software using 5500 markers genotypes present in one or more of five different mapping populations of about 250 RILs.  This reference map was also used in the soybean DNA sequencing effort and the chromosomal bp location of the SNP and SSR markers are now known.  

My research group has created 48 populations of about 200+ F2 plants each that were derived from matings of high x low seed protein parents - ALL F2.3 seed progenies were phenotyped in each population, but ONLY 44 F2 progenitors of the 22 highest and 22 lowest protein F2.3 progenies were selectively genotyped (SG) in each of the 48 F2 populations with about 500 parentally bimorphic markers of the reference map 5500 marker set.

Question 1:  Would it be reasonable to rely solely on the reference genetic map (i.e., marker orders and RIL-based inter-marker Kosambi distances) instead of each actual F2 map (i.e., marker orders and F2-based distances in each of the 48 SG pops) for conducting R/qtl pro & oil interval QTL analyses of the 48 F2 pops?  I ask this question because there was what I took to be an indirect mention of this issue in page 65 of the Broman and Sen book that contrasted a reference genetic map with actual genetic maps.  
 
Note to Readers:  Except over small map distances (or over somewhat larger distances when there were missing F2 marker genotype data), I found the chromosomal marker orders in each of the 48 pops to be nearly identical with the chromosomal marker orders in the reference map.  This comparison was done AFTER conducting all of the Broman-recommended R/qtl marker genotype and F2 individual error checking methods mentioned in his R/qtl tutorials.  However, the recombination fraction values (and thus inter-marker map distances) in the actual genetic maps derived from the 44 genotypes in each SG'd 48 population are substantively larger (chromosomes are about 50-100 % longer in distance) than the reference map.  I am wondering if this chromosomal map length difference between the reference map and each of the 48 F2 genetic maps is of consequence relative to QTL analysis if the marker orders are the same, and if one can substitute reference map order AND reference map inter-marker map distances for the actual genetic maps in each of the 48 populations?

Question 2:  If one uses a csvr file in which the reference map marker order and it's Kosambi map distances are included with the F2 genotype data (44 of the 200+ F2 plants), how then does one handle the est.rf function for an R/qtl-based QTL analysis wherein some R/qtl commands may require the use of the est.rf function?  I ask this question given that I am inputting the selfed-RIL-based reference map Kosambi inter-marker distances (not the F2 derived distances), yet the execution of the est.rf function will use the F2 marker genotype data.  The observed (selfed) RIL recombination fraction R values are greater than observed F2 recombination values (i.e., per meiosis rf values), but can be related to each other by the standard Haldane and Waddington formula R = [(2r)/(1+2r)].  Does one incur a problem by putting RIL marker order and distances in a csvr file that contains F2 marker genotype data relative to doing a subsequent QTL analysis with the resultant genetic map?

Any replies to this post in the form of comments, opinions, insights, etc would be greatly appreciated.

- Jim

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Substituting a Reference Genetic Map for a given Actual Genetic Map
parts:
Regarding your first question, I would aim to get the true marker order for your cross, which would hopefully be the same between the two maps. I would use the map that you think best reflects the underlying marker order. Regarding distances, if you have reasonably dense marker genotype data (as you seem to, then it shouldn't matter whether you use the reference map or that estimated from your data. And so I would focus on the results: do the analysis both ways, and then if the results are similar, use whatever map is convenient. If the results are quite different, figure out which one you trust.

Regarding your second question, est.rf completely ignores the genetic map and just estimates recombination fraction between pairs of markers with the observed data. But in my view this tool is solely for diagnostic purposes, and so I wouldn't worry about inconsistencies between the results from est.rf and your reference map. But perhaps I'm not understanding your concern.

karl
